body.text: Controversial new defence laws were rushed through parliament. What do they mean?
In short:
Contentious new legislation aimed at tightening security at defence bases has passed parliament, amid criticism of a lack of scrutiny.
The new laws allow for the creation of "defence security zones" in areas where Defence is operating, and those who enter without permission could face jail.
What's next?
The laws have faced criticism about possible overreach, but the government has pushed back against suggestions the powers could be misused.
Significant new legal powers to better protect Australia's defence bases have been quickly pushed through parliament, attracting some controversy in the process.
The laws respond to longstanding concerns within the government and Defence that some of Australia's most sensitive defence bases are under-protected, particularly against drones.
But the changes come with remarkable new powers, including the ability to make almost anywhere a temporary "defence zone" and to make almost anyone a "defence security official".
The changes sailed through parliament with the opposition's support, but have drawn criticism from some independents, legal experts, unions and academics.
They point to the possibility of misuse or overreach, and worry the powers could be used to crack down on legitimate protest.
They also argue the bill is massive, running to hundreds of pages, with parliament given just days to scrutinise it.
The government argues that in a more dangerous and uncertain world, new powers are needed to protect Australia's national security infrastructure.
Extraordinary national security powers often draw criticism about overreach, but the government points to oversight mechanisms designed to prevent misuse.
Defence bases and defence 'zones'
The changes will not immediately mean much at most bases, but Defence argues the laws provide the capacity to respond to growing concerns about the security of Australia's defence bases.
One of the primary concerns is drones. Earlier this year, drones breached airspace over RAAF Base Williamtown, home to most of Australia's F-35 fighter jets.
There has been a surge in drone incidents at bases over the past few years, from fewer than two dozen reported in 2022-23 to 246 since the middle of last year.
Other air force bases, such as RAAF Base Darwin, have experienced security breaches in just the past few months.
The new laws dramatically expand the powers of Defence personnel to take down drones over their airfields.
But they go much further than that in a few different ways.
One is the declaration of new "defence security zones", a power held specifically by the defence minister.

These new zones could, in theory, be just about anywhere, described in a parliamentary committee report as "an area of land in Australia, the sea, seabed and subsoil in or adjacent to Australia, airspace (excluding outer space) in or adjacent to Australia; a place, building or structure in Australia".
Essentially, it gives Defence the flexibility to protect its operations wherever they might be, such as training exercises, testing or manufacturing sensitive technology.
There is a requirement within the legislation to consult with anyone "reasonably likely" to be impacted by the declaration.
But it is effectively meaningless, as the minister's decision stands even if that consultation does not happen.
Anyone who enters a defence zone without permission could get two years in prison.
If it is a "special" defence zone, like Pine Gap or the Woomera testing range, the penalty is up to seven years.
Necessary flexibility or executive overreach?
The government argues defence zones are a necessary power to provide the flexibility to protect ADF operations wherever they are needed.
In a statement, a government spokesperson pushed back on criticism these powers could be misused.
"The bill does not give the defence minister power to turn almost anything into a security zone, or declare zones over arbitrary locations," they said.
"It must be based on the existence of a defence capability, activity or security requirement."
But critics of the bill argue the legislation is so broad it could be applied in a remarkably large number of ways.
Independent senator David Pocock has criticised both the bill itself and its hasty progression through the parliament.
"This is so broad it could be used for anything,"

"It could be used around AUKUS bases; it could be used around data centres, anywhere really where the government — or potentially at the request of the United States or someone else who's doing things here — the defence minister could just say, 'Right, no Australians can go to this place.'
"And if they do, if they protest, we can slap you with up to seven years in jail."

The bill does contain protections around the right to protest, with specific provisions stating that action cannot be taken against a person simply for protesting, unless there was a risk of serious harm to people or property.
But those provisions have been criticised by groups like the Maritime Union, who argue they contain too many loopholes.
During the brief parliamentary inquiry into the bill, a senior Defence official suggested the laws could be used to try and manage protests at events like the Land Forces defence expo.
These expos tend to attract significant protests and, as a result, a major police presence.
Defence later clarified that events like Land Forces would not meet the test for a new defence security zone.

"The bill is not intended to support the routine declaration of Defence Security Zones for general industry conferences or exhibitions … the presence of Defence personnel, assets or equipment at an event would not, of itself, satisfy [the] threshold."
Greens leader David Shoebridge argues the bill is still much too far-reaching.
"This legislation is going to war against democracy; it's going to war against our own civil rights," he said.
Criticism of speedy process
The bill was introduced to parliament on October 27, and passed (with amendments) less than a month later.
Because it had the opposition's support, the government had the numbers it needed in both chambers to stop attempts to slow its progress.
But the timeline has drawn criticism from figures like constitutional lawyer Anne Twomey, who argues it is complex legislation that needed more time.
"It is not an appropriate level of scrutiny, particularly for a bill of this kind, that does some serious things," she said.

"It makes significant criminal offences in relation to dealing with defence areas — and that is fine, we should have those offences — but there are also a lot of slippery definitions about mobile defence zones, emergency defence zones and special defence zones, that are not in ordinary places where a defence facility is.
"There could be areas that you just don't know [is] a defence zone, and yet you are doing something in that zone that causes you to commit a criminal offence.
"There is discussion that needs to be had around the edges of this, what the definitions are, how far they go. It went through far too quickly, and that is what people are concerned about."
The bill has also come under scrutiny for the creation of new "defence security officials".
The new Defence officials will have a range of powers to protect defence zones, including to arrest and detain people, request identification, and search people where required.
Defence says it does not want to duplicate the police force, and Defence security officials will not be tasked with carrying out the ordinary work of police.
Anyone taking on the role will have to meet minimum training and qualifications requirements, similar to military police or air force security roles.
Australian Federal Police officers would also take on the powers, where they are tasked with providing security at sensitive bases like HMAS Stirling in WA.
Defence says there is still work to do to establish how the new officials will be appointed and what sort of training they will undergo.
There have been suggestions from some, including senators Shoebridge and Pocock, that the bill would allow American officials to be appointed as Defence security officials.
But the government has pushed back, arguing that it is clearly ruled out in the new laws.
"Foreign defence personnel, including from the United States, cannot be given the powers that apply in Defence Security Zones," a spokesperson said.
Oversight of the new laws
The new laws do come with a layer of oversight to ensure the significant new powers are not misused.
The task primarily falls to the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force (IGADF), essentially the independent office that oversees all of Defence's activities here and abroad.
It is probably best known for the Afghanistan Inquiry, looking into allegations of war crimes committed by Australians abroad.
There are specific reporting rules in the laws ensuring that the IGADF is told when a new defence zone is created and why it is being done.
There is a role for the parliament too, particularly the joint committee on Defence, which has the capacity to hear classified evidence.
But that committee has been criticised by crossbenchers in the past, as its membership is made up only of Labor and Coalition MPs.
